title: Harmonic drives in production: How to specify, verify, and mount the interface
summary: Harmonic drives only hit their backlash and torque numbers if the machined housing and interface are specified right. How to spec, mount, and qualify.
body_markdown:
A harmonic drive can arrive with excellent catalog backlash figures and still perform poorly once it’s installed. A few microns of debris under a bearing seat, some distortion in a thin-wall housing, a mounting bore that’s slightly off the intended axis, any of these can shift the geometry the reducer was designed around.


The gearbox manufacturer controls the wave generator, flexspline and circular spline. You control everything around them: housing, bearing seats, output flange, pilots, bolt patterns and mounting faces. Those surrounding parts decide whether the gearset actually operates in the geometry its torque, stiffness and life numbers were established for.


A harmonic drive pairs very low backlash with a high single-stage ratio in a compact coaxial package.


So integration is as much a manufacturing problem as a gearbox-selection one. The interface has to be pulled from the reducer manufacturer’s installation requirements, translated into functional drawing controls, verified on the machined part, and protected against any change that quietly alters the assembled condition.


The three main components of a harmonic drive. The elliptical wave generator rotates and deforms the flexspline into a mesh with the circular spline at two points. With a 2-tooth difference, each wave-generator revolution advances the flexspline 2 teeth relative to the circular spline. With the circular spline fixed, the flexspline is the output.


## What is a harmonic drive?


A harmonic drive is a


[strain-wave gear](https://www.britannica.com/technology/Harmonic-Drive) uses three main elements: a wave generator, a flexspline and a circular spline.


The flexspline is a thin, flexible cup with external teeth, and it has fewer teeth than the rigid circular spline surrounding it. An elliptical wave generator deforms the flexspline so its teeth mesh with the circular spline at two points, 180° apart.


As the wave generator turns, those two engagement zones sweep around the circumference. Because the flexspline has fewer teeth than the circular spline, it creeps relative to it by a small amount on every revolution of the wave generator.


A common setup uses a flexspline with two fewer teeth than the circular spline. With the circular spline held fixed, that tooth-count difference alone produces a large reduction in a single stage – a 50-tooth flexspline against a 52-tooth circular spline gives 25:1. Commercial units cover a much wider band than that single example, with single-stage ratios commonly running from about 30:1 up to 320:1.


The appeal is obvious: high reduction in a compact coaxial package, low lost motion, high torque density. That’s why you see them in robot joints, cobots,


[spaceflight actuators](https://ntrs.nasa.gov/citations/19830016614) , semiconductor tools, and precision medical or imaging mechanisms. Mounting matters for the same reason: the flexspline is designed to be compliant, and its deformation is what produces the reduction.


This shows the flexspline from the drive example we are using, fractured due to flexing, which results from high cyclic stress due to overload or misalignment.


## Why engineers choose harmonic drives


Low backlash is the trait everyone associates with harmonic drives, but “zero backlash” is a phrase worth being careful with. The architecture genuinely produces very low mechanical backlash next to a conventional gear train – but the output still shows elastic deformation, hysteresis, bearing compliance, and whatever the mounting structure contributes on top. For a positioning system, the number that usually matters is lost motion under changing torque.


High single-stage ratios are the other draw. One stage can replace what would otherwise take two, keeping the motor, reducer and output on a shared axis – useful anywhere joint diameter and mass are tight.


Efficiency is where you give something back. Published figures sit around 75–90%, against roughly 95–98% for planetary gearing under good conditions, and actual numbers move with size, ratio, load, speed, temperature and lubrication. Back-driving efficiency is usually worse still, which matters anywhere the output needs to drive the motor – manual movement, force interaction, regen, or a safety behavior that depends on it.


The flexspline’s constant elastic cycling also puts fatigue at the center of reducer life. A mounting error that shifts flexspline alignment changes the stress the flexspline sees on every cycle.


## Harmonic drive vs. planetary vs. cycloidal reducers


There’s no reducer architecture that wins for every robot or actuator.


Characteristic Harmonic / Strain Wave Planetary Cycloidal


Backlash Very low Low to moderate, grade-dependent Low


Single-stage ratio High Usually lower High


Efficiency Moderate Generally high Moderate to high, design-dependent


Torque density High High High


Shock-load capability Application and size dependent Good in suitable designs Often a strong point


Packaging Coaxial, compact Coaxial Commonly coaxial


Main integration sensitivity Alignment, housing stiffness, flexspline mounting Gear/bearing alignment Eccentric/bearing and output geometry


A precision joint with tight packaging and very little allowable lost motion tends to favor strain-wave – the same tradeoff shows up directly in


[modern harmonic-drive actuator research for robotic joints](https://arpi.unipi.it/retrieve/fb728d55-e026-49de-b625-8597a8b5c422/actuators-14-00492-v2.pdf) . A drivetrain where efficiency, cost and continuous rotation dominate tends to favor planetary. A high-torque joint that has to absorb shock loading often points toward cycloidal.


Make the comparison at the actual duty point – size, ratio, output torque, acceleration, duty cycle, life target and shock loading all move the answer. For a harmonic drive specifically, fold in the housing and output structure needed to install it, since the reducer doesn’t do anything on its own.


## How to specify the harmonic-drive interface on the drawing


Start from the reducer manufacturer’s installation drawing. It sets the mounting diameters, pilots, bolt circles, fits and other geometry the gearbox is designed around – treat those as functional inputs to the housing or flange, not something to redraw approximately off the catalog model.


From there, build a datum structure that reflects how the reducer actually behaves once it’s assembled into the joint.


**Anchor the datums to the axis of rotation.** The primary rotational axis usually comes from a pilot, bearing seat, or other cylindrical feature that sets the gearset’s position. Mounting faces then set axial location and orientation. Bolt patterns clamp things together, but shouldn’t be relied on to


*locate* a precision reducer where a dedicated pilot or bearing feature is doing that job – a bolt pattern can sit dead-on within its positional tolerance while the functional pilot is off relative to the bearing seat, and both features can pass inspection individually while the assembled system still has an alignment error.


[ASME Y14.5](https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/y14-standards) GD&T – runout, total runout, perpendicularity, position – exists to control exactly these relationships, and it’s worth applying only where it maps to a real functional requirement rather than added to make the drawing look thorough.


**Mounting bores and bearing seats** need controlled size and geometry.


[ISO 286](https://www.iso.org/standard/45975.html) fit classes are a useful framework where standardized hole-and-shaft fits apply, but the actual fit has to come from the bearing, the reducer, and the assembly requirements – a generic H7 bore isn’t automatically right just because it’s a familiar callout. Whether the fit needs clearance, transition, or interference depends on load, material and thermal behavior. The same goes for a nominal ±0.01 mm tolerance: a shop hitting it doesn’t mean it’s the tolerance this interface actually needs. Use the manufacturer’s mounting spec where one exists, and derive anything beyond it from the assembly tolerance stack.


**The output flange and bolt pattern** carry torque from the reducer into the driven structure, so the pilot, mounting face and bolt pattern all need to stay geometrically tied to the output axis. A flange can have a dead-accurate bolt circle and still run eccentric if its pilot relationship is wrong – the datum scheme should make that combination impossible within the allowed stack. In a robot joint, a small error here doesn’t stay local; it propagates into the next link and shows up as end-effector positioning error, which is one reason inspection shouldn’t stop at individual dimensions.


**Surface finish** belongs on bearing seats, seal running surfaces and precision mounting faces, with the Ra value coming from the bearing, seal or reducer manufacturer’s requirement plus the selected fit. Finishing every machined surface to that level adds cost without adding anything to reducer performance – put the requirement where the interface needs it, and nowhere else. Mating faces also need protection after machining; a surface can leave the CNC in spec and pick up a raised ding in handling that holds the assembly apart just enough to matter.


**General tolerances.**[ISO 2768](https://www.iso.org/standard/7748.html) covers unspecified features reasonably well where the drawing and contract framework use it, but critical harmonic-drive interfaces shouldn’t fall back on a general tolerance just because their nominal dimension happens to appear on the print. The pilot that locates the reducer, the bearing seats, the output datums and the critical mounting faces should carry the controls the assembly actually needs – everything else (tapped holes, cable features, covers, external profile) doesn’t need to match that precision, and tightening it anyway just slows the shop down without buying anything.


Drawing callouts for a harmonic drive manufacturing drawing can be complex, but full specification of all controlled/inspected aspects is the only way to ensure final acceptance and in-application performance.


## Thin-wall housings can change after machining


Robot and aerospace housings are usually designed light, which means thin walls, large pockets, and small sections connecting the bearing and reducer interfaces – geometry that can move during manufacturing.


Clamping can distort a thin housing while it’s still on the machine; finish a precision bore in that state and it can change shape the moment the fixture releases. Material removal can also release residual stress – pulling a large pocket out of one side of an aluminum billet can shift a bearing seat that was already machined earlier in the sequence.


The machining plan has to account for the finished, free-state geometry, which on sensitive parts can mean rough machining, an intermediate relaxation step, semi-finishing, and final machining – the right sequence depends on material, wall thickness, stock condition and tolerance. Workholding needs the same attention: clamp enough to support the part, not so much that it forces the critical interface into a shape it can’t hold once released. For very tight interface geometry, inspecting the part unclamped matters too – a CMM reading taken under different constraints than the assembled condition can end up answering the wrong question.


## Housing stiffness affects reducer performance


Dimensional accuracy only covers part of the mounting problem. The structure holding the circular spline also needs to be stiff enough for the reducer to deliver its rated performance – Harmonic Drive’s own documentation flags housing stiffness as a factor in ratcheting torque.


Ratcheting happens when excessive torque forces tooth engagement past the reducer’s allowable condition. The limit is specific to reducer size and configuration, so pull it from the manufacturer’s data for your unit.


The Harmonic Drive catalog \[link: Harmonic Drive catalog page\] bases rated and peak torque on infinite flexspline fatigue life and puts buckling at roughly 16–17× rated torque. Treat those figures as illustrative and confirm them for the size you select.


A tighter bore tolerance won’t fix this. A perfectly machined housing that’s too flexible can still let the reducer run outside its intended geometry under load. Your design review needs to cover the unloaded interface geometry and the loaded structural behavior.


## Cleanliness before assembly


A small particle trapped between two precision mounting faces creates a local offset, and if that face sets the circular spline or bearing alignment, the error goes straight into the gearset. Deburr the interface features, clean the mating surfaces, and inspect them before assembly – a part arriving in protective packaging isn’t automatically ready for precision assembly just because it looks clean.


Thread debris deserves the same attention: chips left in tapped holes can stop fasteners from reaching their intended clamp load, or migrate into nearby bearings and lubricated components. Lubrication itself – grease type, quantity, distribution – comes from the reducer manufacturer and should be treated as a controlled assembly input wherever the selected reducer specifies it, since it affects efficiency, temperature and life.


## Verification starts with the machined interface


A CMM report earns its keep here because it verifies the relationships that matter


*before* the reducer goes in. The inspection plan should follow the functional datum system on the drawing – bore size, position, mounting-face orientation, pilot geometry, bolt-pattern location, runout – each tied directly to a drawing requirement. A ballooned drawing gives first article inspection its characteristic map, and for controlled production the FAI package should connect each characteristic to its measurement result along with the material and processes used.


But dimensional verification is only the first stage. The assembled reducer has performance characteristics an empty housing simply can’t show you.


**Backlash and lost motion.** Backlash on a precision reducer is an angular quantity, reported in arc-minutes or arc-seconds depending on the reducer and test method. One arc-minute is 1/60 of a degree, and one arc-second is 1/3,600 of a degree. USPTO patent 10084362 \[link: USPTO 10084362\] treats backlash under 3 arc-min as high precision, against 3–15 arc-min for an ordinary planetary gearbox.


Lost-motion testing applies torque through a defined cycle while measuring the angular displacement between input and output, and the resulting curve captures mechanical lost motion together with elastic torsional deformation and hysteresis – which is why a torque-vs-angular-displacement plot tells you more than a single backlash number ever will. Fixture stiffness, applied load, measurement resolution, and whether the reducer is tested alone or inside the production housing can all shift the result. If the acceptance requirement applies to the assembled actuator, test the assembled actuator.


**Torsional stiffness under load.** A reducer can have almost no mechanical backlash and still deflect meaningfully under torque –


[ongoing JPL research into direct joint-torque measurement on flexspline flanges](https://www.jpl.nasa.gov/site/research/media/posters/2020/R20250p.pdf) exists precisely because this elastic behavior is hard to observe any other way – and that elastic behavior contributes directly to positioning error under load – for robot control, this can matter as much as no-load repeatability, since a joint carrying a long arm sees torque-dependent angular displacement even with negligible tooth clearance. Stiffness isn’t a fixed number either; it moves with reducer size, ratio, torque region and construction, so use the manufacturer’s data for the specific unit. And the housing and output flange add compliance of their own – where the stiffness requirement is demanding, look at the whole load path: reducer, housing, bearings, flange, fasteners, and the structure around them.


**Concentricity and runout after assembly.** Parts can each pass inspection and still assemble badly – tolerance stack-up, contamination, incorrect seating or assembly technique can all introduce error after the CMM report is signed off. Mounted runout is a useful check wherever the application is sensitive to the final rotational axis, but “check runout” isn’t a production instruction on its own – specify what’s rotating, what sets the reference axis, where the measurement reads, and what the acceptance criterion is. For demanding assemblies, verification typically moves from part inspection to mounted geometric inspection and finally to reducer performance testing, and each stage tends to catch a different class of problem.


Torque versus angular deflection for a harmonic drive, in arc-seconds. Backlash is the tooth-to-tooth clearance, and on a harmonic drive it is very low. Lost motion is the system figure: backlash plus the elastic windup of the flexspline and other parts under load, which is what this loop traces. Check the manufacturer's data for the grade you select.


## What causes harmonic-drive failures?


Flexspline fatigue comes with the territory – the flexspline changes shape on every revolution the wave generator makes, and stress concentrates at points including the tooth root and the transition into its attachment structure, with the exact distribution depending on the specific design and load. Academic tooth-interference analysis of strain-wave gearing has looked at exactly


[how flexspline and circular-spline tooth profiles interact under this repeated deformation](https://petit.lib.yamaguchi-u.ac.jp/14354) .


Mounting error adds to that cycle directly. If the circular spline, flexspline and wave generator don’t share the geometry they were designed around, the flexspline can end up loaded unevenly – manufacturer guidance is consistent that non-concentric mounting shortens service life and contributes to fatigue failure. That link has a cost. A misaligned housing can scrap the reducer mounted in it. If it ships, the same error becomes a field failure and a requalification of the actuator.


Beyond that: tooth wear tends to trace back to loading, lubrication, contamination or alignment; wave-generator bearing fatigue can reflect duty cycle and load, but installation conditions are worth checking during any failure analysis too; and ratcheting under excessive torque is its own distinct failure mode, with manufacturer-published, size- and ratio-specific limits – there’s no useful universal multiple to design against here, only the number for the actual reducer.


## Troubleshooting the interface before blaming the reducer


When an actuator misses backlash, vibration or life targets, start with the assembled geometry rather than the gearset. Confirm the reducer is fully seated. Check the mounting faces for burrs, debris and raised damage. Verify the pilot and bearing relationships against the drawing. Measure output runout if the application calls for it.


Then look at assembly conditions – fastener torque and sequence matter more on thin or compliant housings, and a circular spline clamped into a distorted interface won’t behave like the same part installed in the manufacturer’s reference structure. Lubrication and contamination are worth ruling out before concluding the gearset itself is at fault.


For a recurring production issue, compare failing assemblies against known-good units and work backward through the part records. A change in machining sequence, material condition, supplier, surface treatment or assembly process can turn out to be the real cause – one that’s invisible if you only look at the reducer’s part number.


## Fitting the interface into the production quality system


Once an actuator is qualified, the job shifts from proving one assembly works to reproducing the same controlled interface at volume. Your approved vendor list (AVL) belongs in the same controlled set. A housing qualified at one shop stays tied to that shop until you approve a change.


First article inspection is how a new supplier proves to you that it can hit the required characteristics. Depending on the program, the package can include a ballooned drawing, dimensional results, material certificates, CoCs and process records. Aerospace work may call for


[AS9102](https://www.sae.org/standards/content/as9102c/) AI inside an AS9100-controlled supplier system. Other programs run under ISO 9001 and use PPAP or a customer-specific approval process. That takes one point of accountability for the interface parts: someone who owns the FAI package and the qualified process behind it.


Here is where a silent supplier does damage. Mid-program, a shop changes the machining route on a qualified housing, the dimensions still pass, and the residual stress and distortion shift underneath them. You find out when an assembled actuator misses its backlash or life target.


Any change to the qualified process, including material substitutions, needs your engineers’ review before parts ship.


With Jiga as your supplier of record, you talk directly to the shop machining your housing, and someone at Jiga owns the order. Revision mismatches and silent route changes get caught and brought to your engineers before parts ship.


## Supplier approval checklist for harmonic-drive interface machining


Whether you qualify shops yourself or Jiga qualifies them for you, check that:


- They have the reducer manufacturer’s current installation requirements.


- Critical pilots, bearing seats and mounting faces are explicitly controlled on the drawing.


- The datum scheme follows the functional rotational and mounting interfaces.


- Bearing and pilot fits reference the applicable design requirement, not an arbitrary shop default.


- Critical bolt patterns are related to the functional datum system.


- Surface-finish requirements are applied only where the interface needs them.


- Thin-wall features have been reviewed for machining and clamping distortion.


- The machining sequence accounts for residual-stress movement where it’s relevant.


- Inspection verifies the part in the condition the drawing requires.


- CMM capability matches the required geometric controls.


- Mating surfaces are deburred, cleaned and protected before shipment.


- Material certification and lot traceability are available where required.


- FAI requirements are agreed before first production.


- Ballooned drawing and characteristic-accountability records are available where required.


- CoCs and process certifications ship with the part, ready at receiving.


- Revision control covers the drawing, customer specifications and reducer interface data.


- Deviations affecting mounting geometry require engineering approval.


- The supplier can support repeat production and the required inspection volume.


- Alternates are pre-qualified across regions before an interruption forces an uncontrolled source change.


For a robotics or aerospace actuator, Jiga is your manufacturing arm for the housings, bearing interfaces, output flanges and other machined structures around the reducer. Jiga owns getting those parts made by qualified suppliers, and the harmonic-drive manufacturer stays the authority on the gearset

## Frequently Asked Questions


What is a harmonic drive and how does it work?


A harmonic drive is a strain-wave gear reducer that uses a wave generator, flexible spline and rigid circular spline to produce a high reduction ratio in a compact coaxial package. The wave generator deforms the flexspline into engagement with the circular spline, and because the two splines differ in tooth count, rotating the wave generator produces slow relative movement of the flexspline. A common arrangement uses a flexspline with two fewer teeth than the circular spline.


Harmonic drive vs. planetary vs. cycloidal: which reducer suits a robot joint?


Harmonic drives shine where compact packaging, high reduction ratio and very low lost motion matter most. Planetary and cycloidal reducers trade those strengths for different combinations of efficiency, stiffness, cost and shock-load capability. The right call depends on the actual joint requirements – output torque, ratio, acceleration, positioning performance, duty cycle, back-drive behavior, available volume and expected shock loading – and should include the housing and output structure, since those add mass, compliance and cost of their own.


Why do harmonic drives have near-zero backlash?


Strain-wave gearing keeps multiple teeth engaged at once and avoids the tooth clearance that accounts for most backlash in a conventional gear train. “Near-zero” is the more honest phrase, though – an assembled reducer still shows lost motion, elastic deformation and hysteresis, small enough that they’re usually measured in arc-minutes or arc-seconds. The acceptance value depends on the selected reducer and the system requirement, not a generic harmonic-drive number.


How do you tolerate a harmonic-drive housing and bearing seat?


Start with the reducer and bearing manufacturers’ mounting requirements, then control the functional relationships with a datum scheme and appropriate fits and GD&T. ISO 286 covers standardized fits where they apply, and ASME Y14.5 provides the geometric controls for bearing seats, pilots, mounting faces and bolt patterns. There’s no single “correct” harmonic-drive housing tolerance – reducer size, bearing arrangement, housing material, temperature, load and assembly method all factor into what the interface actually needs, and the goal is simply reproducing the alignment the reducer’s design assumes.


What causes harmonic-drive failure?


Flexspline fatigue, tooth wear, wave-generator bearing fatigue, overload and mounting error are the main mechanisms. The mounting structure can contribute directly – non-concentric installation shifts flexspline alignment, and insufficient housing stiffness can change how well the circular spline is supported under torque. Failure investigation should look at the custom housing and assembly geometry, not just the purchased reducer, which is where dimensional records earn their value: a housing’s CMM report, material record, assembly history and revision status give an investigation somewhere to start when a reducer fails early.
